prompt:
Write a technical description of about 800 words of how Git stores a commit, covering blobs, trees, commit objects and refs. The reader is a developer who uses Git every day and has never looked inside the .git directory.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Everything Git remembers about your project lives in a directory called .git at the root of the working tree, and the heart of it is a plain key-value store in .git/objects where each value is a compressed blob of bytes and each key is the SHA-1 or SHA-256 hash of that content, prefixed by a small header giving the object's type and size. Because the key is computed from the content, identical content always lands under the same name, nothing stored can be altered without changing its name, and two files with the same bytes anywhere in your history cost the space of one. A freshly written object sits in a file whose path is the first two hex characters of the hash as a directory and the remaining characters as the filename, so an object beginning a94a8f is found at .git/objects/a9/4a8f and so on, although after enough activity or a git gc, Git folds many of these loose files into packfiles under .git/objects/pack, where similar objects are stored as deltas against one another.

There are four kinds of object, and the first is the blob, which holds the contents of one file and nothing else, with no filename, no permissions and no timestamps. If you rename a file or copy it to another directory its blob is unchanged, which is why Git can later notice renames by comparing content rather than by tracking them explicitly. Names and modes belong to the second kind, the tree, which represents a directory as a list of entries, each pairing a file mode such as 100644 for a regular file, 100755 for an executable or 040000 for a subdirectory with a name and the hash of the object it points to. An entry for a file points to a blob and an entry for a subdirectory points to another tree, so a whole project snapshot is a tree of trees whose root hash summarizes every byte beneath it; change one character in one file deep in the hierarchy and the blob hash changes, which changes the hash of its containing tree, and so on up to the root, while every untouched sibling subtree keeps its old hash and is shared with the previous snapshot. This is why a commit that alters three lines adds only a handful of small new objects rather than a copy of the repository.

The third kind is the commit, a short text object containing the hash of a root tree, zero or more parent commit hashes, an author and a committer each with a name, email, timestamp and timezone, and then a blank line followed by the message. A commit therefore does not store a diff at all, because it points at a complete snapshot, and the diffs you see in git show or in a pull request are computed on demand by comparing the commit's tree with its parent's tree. The parent lines turn isolated snapshots into history, since an ordinary commit has one parent, the first commit in a repository has none and a merge commit has two or more, so the whole history forms a directed acyclic graph in which each commit's hash covers its parents' hashes and thereby the entire ancestry behind it, which is why amending or rebasing a commit produces new hashes for every descendant. The fourth object type, the annotated tag, is a similar small record that names another object, usually a commit, and adds a tagger, a message and optionally a signature.

Hashes are unwieldy for people, so Git layers refs on top, and a ref is nothing more than a file containing a hash. Your branches are files under .git/refs/heads, so main is the file .git/refs/heads/main holding the forty hex characters of the commit at the tip of that branch, tags live under .git/refs/tags, and the remote-tracking branches that git fetch updates live under .git/refs/remotes. When you make a commit, Git writes the new commit object with the old tip as its parent and then overwrites the branch file with the new hash, which is all that advancing a branch means, and for the same reason creating a branch is nearly free, since it writes one tiny file, while deleting one removes only the label and leaves the commits in the object store until garbage collection finds them unreachable. HEAD, found at .git/HEAD, is usually not a hash but a symbolic ref reading something like ref: refs/heads/main, meaning that the current branch is main and that the next commit should move it; when you check out a specific commit instead, HEAD holds a raw hash, which is the detached state Git warns you about because new commits then have no branch file keeping them reachable.

Between your working directory and the object store sits the index, the binary file .git/index, which records for every tracked path its mode, its blob hash and some file-system metadata, so that git add writes blobs into the object database immediately and updates the index, and git commit builds tree objects from the index, wraps the root tree in a commit object and moves the current branch. You can watch all of this by running git cat-file -p with a hash or a name such as HEAD, which prints a commit, then its tree, then the blobs beneath it, and doing that once makes the everyday commands feel much less mysterious.
